content: For both feeding groups, nuts were allowed. For non-breastfed children, the intake of nuts and seeds approached the maximum permissible amount. Eliminating specific food groups or subgroups had minimal impact on the macronutrient profiles of infants. At 9 months of age, the effects were similarly limited. The most significant changes in macronutrient distribution occurred when both fruits and vegetables were excluded, resulting in increased protein intake and decreased carbohydrate intake. The estimated energy requirements were calculated as averages for boys and girls at the midpoint of the age range and at the 50th percentile for weight-for-age. Scenarios with no significant differences from the all food groups scenario were omitted. Shaded cells in the data tables indicate values that fall outside the Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Ranges (AMDR): protein (5–20%), fat (30–40%), and carbohydrates (45–65%). However, due to the limitations of the Optifood model, which outputs macronutrient values in grams rather than kilocalories, Atwater factors were used to convert grams to kilocalories and then to percentages of energy. Additionally, the primary food composition database reports total carbohydrates rather than available carbohydrates. These factors introduce imprecision into the macronutrient energy percentage estimates, which may sum to more than 100%. While these estimates provide a general overview, values exceeding or falling below the AMDR should be interpreted cautiously unless the deviation is substantial. When vegetables were eliminated, there was an increase in dairy and protein foods, likely to compensate for iron and other mineral needs. Eliminating flesh foods (e.g., meat, liver, poultry, fish) led to increased consumption of dairy and plant-based protein foods. Staple foods consistently remained at the stipulated minimum number of daily servings per week across all scenarios. For older infants, eliminating whole-grain staple foods reduced starchy staple foods to the minimum level and increased fruit consumption. Removing vegetables led to increased consumption of dairy and starchy staple foods, particularly whole grains. Eliminating legumes, nuts, and seeds resulted in increased consumption of whole-grain staples and animal-based protein foods. Excluding liver and small fish led to increased consumption of other animal-based protein foods, while broader elimination of flesh foods increased dairy intake. For infants aged 9 months, starchy staples contributed 26% of energy, with 5 servings per week providing 4% of total energy. The percentage of energy from protein foods tripled, with increases in both animaland plant-based protein sources. This is noteworthy because whole-grain consumption does not dominate starchy staple consumption in many contexts. When vegetables were excluded, starchy staples were reduced to a lesser extent, and both types of protein foods increased significantly. Conversely, when fruits were excluded, starchy staples increased, particularly white roots, tubers, and plantains. When both fruits and vegetables were excluded, there were substantial increases in both animaland plant-based protein foods. Excluding liver and small fish reduced starchy staples from 29% to 9% of energy, while dairy, animal-based protein foods, and plant-based protein foods all increased significantly. This is important because liver and small fish are rarely consumed in many contexts for which data were available. When whole-grain foods were excluded, energy from starchy staples decreased to 16%, and plant-based protein foods increased from 0% to 21% of energy. When vegetables were excluded, both animaland plant-based protein foods increased. When fruits were excluded, starchy staples and plant-based protein foods increased. When both fruits and vegetables were excluded, there was a significant increase in energy from dairy, as well as substantial increases in both animaland plant-based protein foods. When dairy was excluded, starchy staples were slightly reduced, and both animaland plant-based protein foods increased significantly. Eliminating flesh foods had minimal impact on patterns, but removing both flesh foods and eggs reduced staple foods, slightly increased dairy, and increased plant-based protein foods from 0% to 9% of energy. Food group and subgroup diversity remained generally similar to models including all food groups, as other groups were selected when one was eliminated. Restricting staple foods to a single type had minimal impact on macronutrient profiles. For infants aged 9 months, limiting staple foods to roots, tubers, and plantains resulted in higher fat and lower carbohydrate intake. Similar results were observed in the rice-only scenario for non-breastfed infants and young children (IYC). Including unhealthy items had minimal impact on macronutrient profiles for IYC aged 9 months and older. Macronutrient levels remained within acceptable ranges. For 9-month-old infants, including sweetened beverages or sweet biscuits seven days a week resulted in lower protein and higher carbohydrate levels. Less frequent inclusion of unhealthy items, or inclusion of crisps/chips at any frequency, did not significantly alter macronutrient profiles.
